planting.note: Divide rooted horizontal stem sections in spring and press into a thin layer of living sphagnum over constantly saturated sand or peat; water only with rainwater, distilled, or RO water, since dissolved minerals in tap water kill it over time.

directions: This is a specialist bog-garden plant best treated as a companion to Sarracenia and Drosera rather than a casual shade groundcover, with a low, horizontally spreading evergreen texture distinct from the upland forest-floor clubmosses already in cultivation. It competes poorly with anything more vigorous, so keep it isolated in its own open, constantly wet patch of mineral-free peat-over-sand. Source only nursery-propagated divisions with an intact rooted sod block, since wild-collected material without soil has a very high failure rate.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Divide rooted horizontal stems in spring and plant into a thin peat layer over moist sand; use rainwater, distilled, or RO water only, since hard or alkaline water kills it over time.

directions: Named for its arching, fox-tail-like fertile strobilus, this bog clubmoss fills the same wet-acidic-bog niche as its congener Lycopodiella appressa, giving a shaded pond margin or carnivorous-plant display bed a distinctly different form from the upland clubmosses already in cultivation. It is a bog-garden specialist for the carnivorous-plant-hobbyist crowd rather than a general-purpose shade groundcover, and needs a thin peat-over-sand layer kept constantly wet with mineral-free water. Acquire plants only from a source that can confirm nursery propagation rather than wild digging, since eBay listings of this species carry a real risk of being mislabeled wild-collected material.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
